newsitem.title: USA: NCAA-MINNESOTA'S HASKINS NOT SURPRISED TO BE IN FIRST FINAL FOUR.
newsitem.headline: NCAA-MINNESOTA'S HASKINS NOT SURPRISED TO BE IN FIRST FINAL FOUR.

text.p: The only coach who isn't acting surprised to find himself in Saturday night's NCAA basketball tournament Final Four is the only one who has never been there here before.

Early in the season, Rick Pitino had lowered his expectations of another national collegiate basketball title for his defending champion Kentucky Wildcats, thinned by four defections to the NBA and two key injuries.
"I'm very surprised at the way we've developed because quite frankly the preseason for me out of all the years I've been in Kentucky was a nightmare as far as our expectations," Pitino said.
Dean Smith's North Carolina Tar Heels put him atop the all-time wins list among Division I coaches and have won 16 consecutive games, but they started out 0-3 in the Atlantic Coast Conference.
In their first game of the season the Tar Heels suffered an 11-point loss to Saturday's semifinal opponent, Arizona.
"When Arizona and North Carolina met, the first game of the season, both teams were young, and both teams have improved a great deal," Smith said.

Arizona Wildcats coach Lute Olson's team began the season with just as many doubts, and had close calls every step of the way through the NCAA regionals -- including the big one, the toppling of heavy NCAA Tournament favourite Kansas.

"It's been a satisfying year," said Olson. "I don't remember a team that came into a year with so many question marks that could get as far as what they've gotten now. And they feel now that they're one of four, why it could be anybody's game."
By contrast with the other three, Minnesota's Clem Haskins, making his and his school's first appearance in the Final Four, felt maybe people should have seen the Golden Gophers coming.
"I don't know why people don't respect us," he said.

"We have a problem with that. We know we have a fine ball club. Any time you play the Big 10 and you win 16 basketball games you know you've got to be doing something great, great coaches and great players. We do have a good programme and good team.
"But I think other people are beginning to recognise that."
Last year, it was Kentucky who had the depth to throw waves of great players at opponents. But in Saturday night's second game, Minnesota (31-3) will have the numbers against Kentucky (34-4).
"We're here because we had nine players that played double-figure minutes for a ball game, and we're here because of a strong defence, and we've done everything we can to win," said Haskins.
Said Pitino: "Right now we don't have the depth that Minnesota has. But that's something we've been conditioned to go without."

Of course, who needs depth when you have super swingman Ron Mercer? Headed for the NBA Draft after just two years at Kentucky, Mercer has carried the team and averaged 16.5 points in the four NCAA Tournament games.
"Mercer is one of the finest college players, tremendous quickness and speed, and he played great team basketball," said Haskins.

Minnesota has its own, less-heralded superstar -- Bobby Jackson, who scored 54 points in the regional semifinal and final. Haskins says Jackson is "kind of one of the best-kept secrets in basketball. I hope that we can keep it two more basketball games."

Saturday night's first semifinal matchup pits perennial contender North Carolina (28-6) against the surprise of the tournament, Arizona (34-4), which has gotten to the national semifinals twice but never reached a final.
North Carolina has won three NCAA Tournament titles, two under Smith (1982, 1993), and is in the Final Four for the 11th time in his 36-year coaching career.
While Olson raves about the precision of the Tarheels' offence, Smith downplays his team, as is his practice.
"It's been a gradual process and we're still not a great team," Smith said. "I think we're still improving and I hope we can show improvement against Arizona on Saturday."

Serge Zwikker, North Carolina's 7-foot-2 (2.18 meters) senior centre in his third Final Four in four years, could provide the edge in height and experience the Tar Heels will need against the Wildcats, who start no seniors.
"They're a very quick team, and quicker than we are," said Smith. "We have one player with size more than their two 6-11s (2.11 meters) with Serge Zwikker."

The young Arizona team, the only one of the survivors not seeded first in its region, had to learn how to play together, then how to play together anew when their leader, guard Miles Simon, came aboard after missing the first 11 games due to poor academics.
"But without a doubt we're playing the best basketball that we have all year," Olson said.

Kentucky is trying to become just the second team to repeat as NCAA Tournament champion since UCLA's seven-year run ended in 1973. Duke, which won the NCAA Tournament in 1991 and 1992, is the only team to repeat since then.
